lessons.title: Anatomy and Physiology of Rabbits
lessons.body:
Rabbits are small mammals with a lightweight skeleton, making up only about 7-8% of their body weight. This means they are fragile and must be handled carefullyânever lift a rabbit by the ears or scruff. Instead, support the chest with one hand and the hindquarters with the other. Their powerful hind legs can kick hard enough to break their own back if they struggle while unsupported. A healthy adult rabbit weighs between 2 kg (small breeds) and 6 kg (large breeds like Flemish Giant).

Their eyes are positioned on the sides of the head, giving them nearly 360-degree vision to spot predators, but they have a blind spot directly in front of their nose. This is why you should approach them from the side, not head-on. Their ears are large and mobile, acting as heat regulatorsârabbits lose excess body heat through their ears. In hot African climates, this helps them stay cool, but they still need shade and ventilation.

Rabbits have continuously growing teeth (elodonts). The incisors grow about 2-3 mm per week. Without hard food to chew, their teeth can overgrow, causing painful abscesses and starvation. Provide tough hay, branches, or wooden blocks for gnawing. Their digestive system is unique: they are hindgut fermenters and practice coprophagyâeating soft night feces to reabsorb vitamins and proteins. This is normal and essential; never stop a rabbit from eating its cecotropes.

Their respiratory system is delicate. Rabbits are obligate nasal breathersâthey cannot breathe through their mouths. Any nasal blockage from dust, ammonia, or infection can suffocate them. Keep bedding dry and clean. Their heart beats 130-300 times per minute, and body temperature is 38.5-40Â°C. They do not sweat; they pant and use their ears to cool down. In African heat, provide frozen water bottles or shaded burrows. Understanding these basics helps you prevent stress, injury, and disease.

lessons.title: Reproductive System of Male and Female Rabbits
lessons.body:
Male rabbits (bucks) have two testicles that descend into a scrotal sac between the anus and penis. They can retract them into the abdomen when scared or cold, so you may not always see them. A mature buck can mate from 4-5 months for small breeds, 6-7 months for large breeds. The penis is a small tube that protrudes during mating. Bucks are ready to mate almost constantly, but overuse reduces fertility. A healthy buck can serve 1-2 does per week.

Female rabbits (does) have a bicornuate uterusâtwo separate uterine horns, each with its own cervix opening into the vagina. This means a doe can carry two litters at different stages of development, though this is rare. The vulva is the external opening; it changes color from pale pink (not ready) to dark red or purple (ready to mate). This color change is the best way to time mating. Does reach sexual maturity at 4-6 months (small breeds) or 6-9 months (large breeds).

Mating is quickâthe buck mounts, falls off, and grunts. After mating, the doe ovulates 10-12 hours later (induced ovulation). Pregnancy (gestation) lasts 28-32 days. A doe can become pregnant again within hours of kindling (giving birth). To control breeding, keep bucks and does separate except for planned mating. Provide a nesting box with soft hay 25-28 days after mating. Kindling usually happens at night and takes 15-30 minutes. Litters range from 4-12 kits, depending on breed and age.

In African smallholder setups, use a ratio of 1 buck to 10 does. Check the vulva color before matingâif pale, wait 2-3 days. Always take the doe to the buck's cage, not the other way around; does are territorial and may fight. After mating, record the date. If the doe fails to kindle by day 35, re-mate her. Proper reproductive management ensures steady meat production.

lessons.title: Natural Behaviors and Social Structure
lessons.body:
Rabbits are social animals. In the wild, they live in groups called colonies with a strict hierarchy. In your rabbitry, you must mimic this by housing them in compatible pairs or groupsâbut only if space allows. A dominant rabbit will mount, chase, and sometimes bite subordinates. Fighting can cause serious wounds. For beginners, individual cages (60 cm x 60 cm x 45 cm) are safest. If you group house, provide 1 square meter per rabbit and multiple hiding spots.

Rabbits are crepuscularâmost active at dawn and dusk. They sleep during the hottest part of the day. In Africa, this means feeding early morning and late evening when it's cooler. They are territorial, especially does. A doe with kits will defend her nest aggressively. Never put your hand into a nest without checkingâshe may bite. Bucks mark territory with urine and chin rubbing (scent glands under the chin).

Chewing is a natural behavior. Rabbits chew to wear down teeth and to explore. Provide safe chew toys: untreated wood, cardboard, or dried corn cobs. Without chewing outlets, they will destroy cage wire or plastic. Digging is also instinctive. If housed on wire floors, they may dig at the wire, causing foot sores. Provide a solid resting board or a digging box with hay.

Rabbits thump their hind legs as an alarm signal. If you hear a loud thump, check for predators (dogs, snakes, rats) or sudden disturbances. They also grunt when angry or when mating. A high-pitched squeal means pain or fearâhandle gently. In hot climates, rabbits may sprawl flat on their sides to cool down. This is normal, not illness, if they respond to you. Understanding these behaviors reduces stress and improves production.

lessons.title: Digestive System and Nutritional Needs
lessons.body:
Rabbits are hindgut fermenters. Their digestive tract is designed for high-fiber, low-energy forage. The stomach is never emptyâit constantly produces acid. The small intestine absorbs nutrients, then the cecum (a large pouch) ferments fiber with bacteria. Finally, the colon separates hard feces from soft cecotropes. Cecotropes are eaten directly from the anusâthey provide B vitamins and proteins. If a rabbit stops eating cecotropes, it loses vital nutrients.

A rabbit's diet must be 70-80% fiber. In Africa, use locally available feeds: sweet potato vines, cassava leaves (dried to remove toxins), moringa leaves, napier grass, and lucerne (alfalfa) hay. Commercial pellets are convenient but should be limited to 50-100 g per adult per day. Too many pellets cause obesity and enteritis. Fresh clean water is essentialâa rabbit drinks 100-200 ml per kg body weight daily. In heat, they drink more.

Introduce new feeds gradually over 7-10 days. Sudden changes cause diarrhea, which can kill a rabbit in 24 hours. A simple rule: 70% hay/forage, 20% pellets, 10% treats (carrots, apples, banana peelsâsmall amounts). Avoid lettuce, cabbage, and beans; they cause gas. Never feed moldy or wet grass. Provide a mineral lick for calcium and salt.

Feed twice daily: early morning and late evening. Remove uneaten fresh greens after 2 hours to prevent fermentation. Check droppings dailyâhealthy droppings are round, firm, and brown. If you see soft or watery droppings, reduce greens and give hay only. A rabbit that stops eating for 12 hours is an emergency. Keep a syringe and warm water for force-feeding if advised by a vet. Proper nutrition prevents most diseases.

lessons.title: Common Health Indicators in Rabbits
lessons.body:
A healthy rabbit is alert, curious, and has bright eyes. It eats and drinks normally, and produces round, firm droppings. Its fur is smooth, and it breathes quietly through the nose. Body temperature is 38.5-40Â°C. You can check by feeling the earsâthey should be warm but not hot. A sick rabbit may sit hunched in a corner, grind its teeth (pain), or have labored breathing. Early detection saves lives.

Common signs of illness: not eating, no droppings, diarrhea, sneezing, nasal discharge, head tilt, abscesses, or sudden weight loss. In Africa, heat stress is a major killer. Signs include panting, drooling, and lying stretched out. Move the rabbit to shade, wet its ears with cool water, and provide frozen bottles. Do not submerge in waterâthat causes shock.

Check teeth weekly. Overgrown incisors curl into the mouth. Use nail clippers to trim only if trained, or see a vet. Check eyes for cloudiness or dischargeâcould be conjunctivitis from dust. Check ears for mites (crusty brown debris). Treat with ivermectin drops. Check feet for sore hocks (red, bald patches). Provide soft bedding and solid floors.

Vaccination is not common for rabbits in Africa, but keep a quarantine cage for new rabbits (14 days). Disinfect cages with bleach solution (1:10) and rinse well. Control rats and fliesâthey spread disease. A simple health record per rabbit helps track weight, mating, and treatments. If a rabbit dies suddenly, burn or bury it deep. Do not feed it to other animals. Biosecurity is your best defense.

lessons.title: Understanding Rabbit Communication
lessons.body:
Rabbits communicate through body language, sounds, and scent. Learning their signals helps you manage stress and prevent injury. A relaxed rabbit lies stretched out with ears up or slightly back. A curious rabbit stands on hind legs, ears forward. A frightened rabbit flattens its ears against the head and crouches low. If it thumps a hind foot, it is warning of danger. If it grunts or growls, it is angryâback off.

A rabbit in pain may grind its teeth loudly (bruxism), squeal, or become aggressive. A happy rabbit may purr (a soft clicking sound) when petted. A doe calling her kits makes a low clucking sound. Bucks often honk or circle the doe during courtship. These sounds are normal. But a high-pitched scream means extreme fear or painâhandle with care.

Scent marking is common. Rabbits have glands under the chin, in the groin, and in the anal area. They rub their chin on objects to claim territory. Urine spraying is a dominant behavior, especially in unneutered bucks. To reduce spraying, keep bucks separate or consider castration. Does may also spray if stressed. Clean cages regularly to reduce odor.

In African smallholder settings, observe your rabbits daily. Note their ear position, body posture, and sounds. A rabbit that suddenly hides or stops grooming is sick. A rabbit that bites the cage bars is boredâadd chew toys. A rabbit that circles your feet may be hormonal or seeking attention. Never punish a rabbit; it does not understand punishment. Instead, adjust housing, feeding, or companionship. Good communication builds trust and reduces disease.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Rabbit Biology, Behavior and Health for African Rabbit Enterprises

This Practical Reference consolidates the six lessons of the Rabbit Biology and Behavior module into a working field guide for African rabbit farmers. The emphasis is business-first: every biological fact here is translated into a management action that protects stock value, reduces mortality, and improves feed conversion â the three variables that determine whether a rabbit unit is profitable or merely surviving.

Rabbits are among the most efficient small-livestock protein converters available to African smallholders and commercial units alike. A healthy doe can produce 40â60 weaned kits per year under good management, and rabbit meat sells at premium prices in urban markets across Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, Cameroon and South Africa. But rabbits are also biologically fragile in specific, predictable ways. Understanding their anatomy, reproduction, digestion, behavior and communication allows you to design housing, feeding and breeding systems that work with the animal rather than against it.

1. Anatomy and Physiology â What the Body Tells You About Management

Rabbits are lagomorphs, not rodents. The distinction matters commercially: lagomorphs have two pairs of upper incisors (the second pair is small and peg-like), and their teeth grow continuously throughout life. In practice this means rabbits must always have access to fibrous material to wear down teeth. A rabbit fed only soft, pelleted feed or kitchen scraps will develop malocclusion â overgrown teeth that prevent eating and lead to starvation. In African smallholder systems where forage is cheap and abundant, this is rarely a problem; in intensive units, it is a common and expensive welfare failure.

Key physiological facts for the farm:

  • Body temperature: 38.5â39.5 Â°C. Rabbits cannot sweat. They dissipate heat through their ears and by panting. This is why heat stress is the single biggest killer in tropical and semi-arid Africa.
  • Ears: Large surface area, richly vascularised. They act as radiators. In hot climates, long-eared breeds (e.g. Fauve de Bourgogne crosses) tolerate heat better than short-eared ones.
  • Skeleton: Light and fragile relative to muscle mass. The lumbar spine is particularly vulnerable. Never lift a rabbit by the ears or scruff alone â always support the hindquarters. A dropped rabbit with a broken back is a total loss.
  • Respiratory system: Obligate nasal breathers. They cannot breathe through the mouth. This makes them highly susceptible to ammonia fumes from urine-soaked bedding. Ventilation is not optional; it is a survival requirement.

2. Reproductive System â The Engine of Your Business

Rabbit reproduction is the core profit driver. Does are induced ovulators â they ovulate only after mating. This means a doe can conceive at almost any time if mated, and a single mating is usually sufficient. The gestation period is short: 28â32 days, with 31 days the most common average. Kindling (birth) is rapid, usually 10â30 minutes, and kits are born blind, deaf and hairless.

Bucks reach sexual maturity at 5â6 months; does at 4â5 months, though most commercial units wait until 6 months for the first mating to ensure the doe has reached adequate body size. A mature buck can serve 7â10 does per week without fertility decline. Overworked bucks produce thin ejaculate and lower conception rates â a hidden cost that shows up as empty does and lost feed.

Table 1: Reproductive parameters for tropical rabbit production
Parameter Typical range Management implication
Gestation length28â32 daysPrepare nest box on day 27
Litter size (medium breeds)6â10 kitsFoster surplus kits to smaller litters
Weaning age28â35 daysWean at 4â5 weeks in hot climates
Kindling interval (intensive)35â42 daysRe-mate 11â14 days post-kindling
Kindling interval (extensive)60â90 daysLower output but lower doe mortality
Bucks per 10 does1â2Rotate bucks to prevent fatigue
Productive doe lifespan2â3 yearsCull on falling litter size

Source: Adapted from McNitt, J.I. et al. (2013) Rabbit Production, 9th edition, CABI, Wallingford, UK; and FAO (1997) The Rabbit: Husbandry, Health and Production.

3. Natural Behaviors and Social Structure

Rabbits are social, hierarchical and territorial. In the wild they live in warrens with a dominant buck and doe. In captivity, this translates into clear management rules:

  • Group housing of does: Possible if introduced young and given space, but fighting is common when a new adult is introduced. For commercial units, individual cages for breeding does are safer and easier to manage.
  • Bucks must be housed singly. Two mature bucks will fight, often to serious injury or death. This is non-negotiable.
  • Growers can be group-housed from weaning to slaughter, at 8â10 per square metre in deep litter or 6â8 in cages.
  • Rabbits are crepuscular â most active at dawn and dusk. Feed and inspect at these times for best response.
  • They are prey animals. Loud noises, dogs, rats and sudden movements cause panic, injury and sometimes fatal heart attacks. Site your rabbitry away from barking dogs and heavy foot traffic.

4. Digestive System and Nutritional Needs

Rabbits are hindgut fermenters with a well-developed caecum â a fermentation vat that breaks down fibre. They practice caecotrophy: they produce soft, nutrient-rich caecotrophs (night feces) directly from the anus and re-ingest them. This is not a disease or a bad habit; it is essential. It allows rabbits to recover B-vitamins, microbial protein and water. Never prevent a rabbit from eating its caecotrophs. If you see soft feces stuck to the fur or cage floor, it usually means the diet is too rich in starch or too low in fibre.

Practical feeding rules for African conditions:

  • Fibre is the foundation. Aim for 14â18% crude fibre in the total diet. Fresh forage (sweet potato vines, lucerne, desmodium, mulberry, weeds) is excellent and cheap.
  • Protein: 16â18% for growers and lactating does; 12â14% for maintenance.
  • Water: A lactating doe can drink 2â4 litres per day in hot weather. Water scarcity kills milk production within hours.
  • Avoid sudden diet changes. Transition over 5â7 days. Sudden shifts cause enteritis and death, especially in weaners.
  • Never feed mouldy hay or spoiled greens. Rabbits are highly sensitive to mycotoxins.
Table 2: Common health indicators in rabbits â what to check daily
Indicator Healthy Warning sign Likely cause
EyesClear, bright, no dischargeCloudy, weeping, mattedConjunctivitis, snuffles, ammonia
NoseDry, cleanWhite/yellow discharge, sneezingPasteurellosis (snuffles)
EarsUpright, clean insideDrooping, crusty, scratchingEar mites, injury, heat stress
FecesRound, firm, uniformSoft, watery, absentEnteritis, coccidiosis, diet change
UrineCloudy white/yellow (normal)Bloody, thick, darkUrinary infection, urolithiasis
FurSmooth, glossyRough, bald patches, dandruffMites, ringworm, malnutrition
PostureAlert, sitting normallyHunched, teeth grindingPain, GI stasis, dental disease
AppetiteEating and drinkingRefusing feed, no water intakeAny illness â isolate immediately

Source: Compiled from Meredith, A. & Redrobe, S. (2002) BSAVA Manual of Exotic Pets, 4th edition, British Small Animal Veterinary Association; and Quesenberry, K.E. & Carpenter, J.W. (2012) Ferrets, Rabbits and Rodents: Clinical Medicine and Surgery, 3rd edition, Elsevier.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Zoonoses and Handling

Rabbits can transmit tularaemia, ringworm (dermatophytosis), salmonellosis and leptospirosis to humans. Always wear gloves when handling sick animals or cleaning soiled bedding. Wash hands with soap and running water after every contact. Do not allow children to kiss or nuzzle rabbits. Never eat, drink or smoke in the rabbitry. Pregnant women and immunocompromised persons should avoid cleaning nest boxes and handling afterbirth. Any rabbit that dies suddenly should be buried at least 1 metre deep, away from water sources, or incinerated â never sold or consumed.

5. Understanding Rabbit Communication

Rabbits are quiet but highly communicative. Learning their signals allows early intervention and reduces losses:

  • Teeth grinding (soft): Contentment. Loud grinding: Pain â check for injury, dental problems or GI stasis.
  • Thumping hind foot: Alarm or danger. Something has frightened the colony â check for predators or sudden noise.
  • Ear position: Forward = alert and curious. Flat back = fear or aggression. One ear rotated = possible ear mite irritation.
  • Honking / grunting: Usually a buck courting a doe, or a doe defending nesting kits.
  • Lunging and growling: Aggression â usually a doe with a litter, or a buck in a neighbouring cage. Separate if persistent.
  • Chinning: Rubbing the chin on objects to mark territory using scent glands. Normal.
  • Flopping (sudden lying flat): A sign of deep relaxation and safety. A good indicator of a well-managed, low-stress rabbitry.

Quick Reference Checklist for Daily Rabbitry Management

  1. Water first: Check every drinker or bowl â clean, full and functioning. A dry doe stops milking within 12 hours.
  2. Feed with fibre: Provide forage plus concentrate. Never let a rabbit go more than 12 hours without fibrous feed.
  3. Observe every animal: Eyes, nose, ears, feces, posture and appetite. Isolate any suspect animal immediately.
  4. Check ventilation and ammonia: If your eyes sting, the ammonia level is harming the rabbits. Increase airflow.
  5. Inspect nest boxes: Count kits, remove dead ones, check bedding is dry. Handle kits gently and only when necessary.
  6. Record breeding dates: Mark mating date on the cage card. Prepare nest box on day 27. Expect kindling on day 31.
  7. Secure the perimeter: Check for holes, loose wire, rat burrows and dog access. Predator panic is a major cause of abortion and injury.
  8. End-of-day walk-through: Confirm all rabbits are settled, feeders are secure, and any sick animal has been treated or culled per your protocol.

Further Reading â Free Official Resources

  • FAO â The Rabbit: Husbandry, Health and Production (Lebas et al., 1997) â the definitive free manual for tropical rabbit production.
  • FAO â A Manual for the Practical Study of Root-Nodule Bacteria (companion FAO small-livestock resources) â broader small-livestock husbandry context.
  • CABI â Rabbit Production, 9th edition (McNitt et al., 2013) â standard commercial reference; sample chapters available.
  • MSD Veterinary Manual â Rabbits â free, authoritative disease and anatomy reference.
  • World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) â disease notification and biosecurity standards relevant to rabbit health in Africa.

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills Rabbit Farming course. Every lesson is designed to move a learner from subsistence keeping to commercial production â because in African agribusiness, biology is the foundation, but profit is the goal.

quiz.q: What percentage of a rabbit's body weight is its skeleton?
quiz.explanation: Rabbits have lightweight skeletons, making up only about 7-8% of body weight.

quiz.q: How should you lift a rabbit?
quiz.explanation: Supporting the chest and hindquarters prevents spinal injury from kicking.

quiz.q: Why do rabbits have a blind spot in front of their nose?
options: A) Eyes are on sides for wide vision
quiz.explanation: Side-positioned eyes give nearly 360-degree vision but leave a frontal blind spot.

quiz.q: How fast do rabbit incisors grow?
quiz.explanation: Rabbit incisors grow continuously at about 2-3 mm per week.

quiz.q: What is coprophagy?
quiz.explanation: Coprophagy is eating soft cecotropes to reabsorb vitamins and proteins.

quiz.q: Why can't rabbits breathe through their mouths?
options: B) They are obligate nasal breathers
D) They only breathe through skin
quiz.explanation: Rabbits are obligate nasal breathers, so nasal blockage can suffocate them.

quiz.q: What is the normal body temperature of a rabbit?
quiz.explanation: Rabbit body temperature ranges from 38.5 to 40Â°C.

quiz.q: How many testicles does a male rabbit have?
quiz.explanation: Male rabbits have two testicles that can retract into the abdomen.

quiz.q: At what age do small breed bucks reach sexual maturity?
quiz.explanation: Small breed bucks mature at 4-5 months, large breeds at 6-7 months.

quiz.q: What does a dark red or purple vulva indicate in a doe?
quiz.explanation: A dark red or purple vulva means the doe is ready to mate.

quiz.q: How long is rabbit gestation?
quiz.explanation: Rabbit pregnancy lasts 28-32 days.

quiz.q: What is the recommended buck to doe ratio?
quiz.explanation: One buck can serve about 10 does without fertility loss.

quiz.q: Where should you take the doe for mating?
quiz.explanation: Does are territorial, so take her to the buck's cage to avoid fighting.

quiz.q: When are rabbits most active?
quiz.explanation: Rabbits are crepuscular, active mainly at dawn and dusk.

quiz.q: What does a loud thump mean?
quiz.explanation: Thumping is an alarm signal to warn others of danger.

quiz.q: What is a normal behavior for a rabbit in heat?
quiz.explanation: Rabbits sprawl flat to cool down in hot climates.

quiz.q: What percentage of a rabbit's diet should be fiber?
quiz.explanation: A healthy rabbit diet is 70-80% fiber from hay and forage.

quiz.q: Which feed should be limited to 50-100 g per adult per day?
quiz.explanation: Too many pellets cause obesity and enteritis; limit to 50-100 g daily.

quiz.q: How long should you take to introduce new feeds?
quiz.explanation: Gradual introduction over 7-10 days prevents diarrhea.

quiz.q: Which of these is toxic to rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Undried cassava leaves contain cyanide and are toxic.

quiz.q: What do healthy rabbit droppings look like?
quiz.explanation: Healthy droppings are round, firm, and brown.

quiz.q: What is a sign of heat stress in rabbits?
quiz.explanation: Panting and drooling indicate heat stress; cool the rabbit immediately.

quiz.q: How often should you check a rabbit's teeth?
quiz.explanation: Weekly checks help catch overgrown incisors early.

quiz.q: What causes sore hocks?
quiz.explanation: Wire floors cause pressure sores on the feet; provide solid resting boards.

quiz.q: How long should new rabbits be quarantined?
quiz.explanation: A 14-day quarantine prevents disease introduction.

quiz.q: What does a relaxed rabbit look like?
quiz.explanation: A relaxed rabbit lies stretched out with ears up or slightly back.

quiz.q: What does a high-pitched squeal mean?
quiz.explanation: A squeal indicates extreme fear or pain; handle gently.

quiz.q: Why do rabbits rub their chin on objects?
quiz.explanation: Chin rubbing uses scent glands to claim territory.

quiz.q: What should you do if a rabbit grunts or growls?
quiz.explanation: Grunting or growling means anger; give the rabbit space.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a bored rabbit?
quiz.explanation: Biting cage bars indicates boredom; provide chew toys.
